cards.b: In winter, North American wood frogs can freeze, with ice forming in up to about two-thirds of their body water. Their hearts stop and they stop breathing. In spring they thaw out and hop away, protected by sugar that stops their cells being damaged.

q.p: What do wood frogs do in winter?

rq.p: What protects a frozen frog's cells?

cards.why: High sugar levels act like antifreeze inside cells.

cards.b: Sea otters often sleep floating on their backs, and some hold paws or wrap themselves in kelp so they don't drift apart. A group resting together on the water is called a raft.

q.p: What do sea otters do so they don't drift apart while sleeping?
o: Hold paws or wrap in kelp

rq.p: What is a resting group of sea otters called?

cards.why: Staying together protects them in open water.

cards.b: A 2016 study dated the eye lenses of Greenland sharks and found the oldest was at least 272 years old, possibly much older. That makes them the longest-living vertebrates known. They may not breed until about 150.

q.p: Which vertebrate is the longest-living known?

rq.p: How did scientists estimate the sharks' ages?

cards.why: Very cold water slows their metabolism and growth.

cards.b: When grabbed by a predator, a hagfish releases slime that rapidly expands in seawater into a huge mass of goo, clogging the attacker's gills. Its slime contains fine threads that make it stringy and strong.

q.p: How does a hagfish defend itself?

rq.p: What makes hagfish slime so strong?

cards.why: The slime chokes predators' gills, so they let go.

cards.b: Naked mole-rats live in underground colonies in East Africa and can live over 30 years, far longer than other rodents their size. They very rarely get cancer and can survive for minutes without oxygen.

q.p: How long can naked mole-rats live?

rq.p: Which disease do naked mole-rats very rarely get?

cards.why: Scientists study them to learn about ageing and cancer.

cards.b: In seahorses, the female places her eggs into a pouch on the male's belly. He fertilises and carries them, then gives birth to the babies, sometimes hundreds or more at a time.

q.p: Which seahorse parent gives birth?

rq.p: Where does a male seahorse carry eggs?

cards.why: It's one of the few true male pregnancies in nature.

cards.b: Australia's superb lyrebird is a master mimic. Males copy other birds, and have been recorded imitating camera shutters, car alarms and even chainsaws they've heard. Their elaborate songs help attract mates.

q.p: Which bird has been recorded mimicking chainsaws?

rq.p: Why do male lyrebirds perform complex songs?

cards.why: Females favour males with the most varied songs.

cards.b: When threatened, a bombardier beetle mixes chemicals in a chamber in its abdomen. The reaction heats the mixture to around 100 °C and blasts it out with a popping sound, aimed at the attacker.

q.p: What does a bombardier beetle spray at attackers?

rq.p: How hot is the spray?

cards.why: A chemical reaction releases heat and gas in an instant.

cards.b: Archerfish spit jets of water to knock insects off leaves above the surface, then catch them as they fall. They correct for how light bends at the water's surface, and can hit targets well over a metre away.

q.p: How do archerfish catch insects above water?

rq.p: What do archerfish correct for when aiming?

cards.why: Refraction makes things look shifted from where they really are.

cards.b: Vampire bats can starve after two or three nights without blood. A bat that has fed will often regurgitate blood to a hungry roost-mate, especially one that shared with it before.

q.p: What do well-fed vampire bats do for hungry roost-mates?

rq.p: Who do they share with most?
o: Bats that shared with them before

cards.why: Helping those who've helped you is called reciprocity.

cards.t: Horned lizards squirt blood from their eyes
cards.b: Some horned lizards can squirt a stream of blood from the corners of their eyes, up to over a metre. The blood tastes foul to dogs and coyotes, which back off.

q.p: What can some horned lizards squirt from their eyes?

rq.p: Which predators is the trick mainly aimed at?

cards.why: Chemicals in the blood taste awful to canines.

cards.b: Cuttlefish can change colour and pattern in a fraction of a second to hide or signal. Strangely, their eyes have only one type of colour receptor, so they're thought to be colour-blind. How they match backgrounds is still being studied.

q.p: What's strange about cuttlefish camouflage?

rq.p: How fast can a cuttlefish change colour?
o: In a fraction of a second

cards.why: Muscles stretch pigment sacs in their skin instantly.

cards.b: Leafcutter ants don't eat the leaves they carry. They chew them into mulch to grow a fungus, which they eat. The ants and fungus depend on each other, and colonies can hold millions of ants.

q.p: What do leafcutter ants do with leaves?

rq.p: What do leafcutter ants actually eat?

cards.why: Ants were farming millions of years before humans.

cards.t: Sloths grow algae in their fur
cards.b: Sloth fur has grooves where algae grow, giving some sloths a greenish tint that helps them hide in trees. Moths and other tiny creatures live in the fur too, making each sloth a mini ecosystem.

q.p: What grows in sloth fur?

rq.p: How does the algae help sloths?

cards.why: Slow movement and damp fur suit the algae perfectly.

cards.t: A narwhal's tusk is a tooth
cards.b: The narwhal's long spiral tusk is actually a tooth that grows through its upper lip. It's usually found in males and can reach around 3 metres. Scientists think it's used in displays and may also sense the water around it.

q.p: What is a narwhal's tusk?

rq.p: Where does the tusk grow out of?

cards.why: The tusk is an extremely long left canine tooth.

cards.t: Crocodiles can't stick their tongues out
cards.b: A crocodile's tongue is held in place by a membrane along the floor of its mouth, so it can't poke it out. A flap at the back of the throat seals off water when it opens its jaws underwater.

q.p: Can crocodiles stick their tongues out?

rq.p: What stops water flooding a crocodile's throat?
o: A flap at the back of the throat

cards.why: The membrane anchors the tongue to the mouth floor.

cards.b: Some penguins, like gentoos and Adélies, build nests from pebbles. Males search for the best stones and present them to females, and stealing pebbles from neighbours' nests is common.

q.p: What do some male penguins give to females?

rq.p: What are the pebbles for?

cards.why: Stone nests keep eggs above meltwater.

cards.b: The basilisk lizard of Central and South America can sprint across water on its hind legs. Its feet slap down fast, trapping air pockets that keep it from sinking, until it slows and has to swim.

q.p: Which lizard can run across water?

rq.p: What keeps a running basilisk afloat?

cards.why: Speed matters: when it slows, it sinks.

cards.t: Moray eels have a second set of jaws
cards.b: Moray eels have a second set of jaws in their throat, called pharyngeal jaws. When they bite prey, these inner jaws shoot forward, grab it and drag it down into the throat.

q.p: What's hidden in a moray eel's throat?

rq.p: What do the inner jaws do?

cards.why: Morays can't create strong suction, so they grab instead.

cards.t: A parasite that replaces a fish's tongue
cards.b: The tongue-eating louse is a small crustacean that enters a fish through its gills, attaches to its tongue and drains its blood until the tongue withers. The louse then stays in its place, working as the fish's new tongue.

q.p: What does the tongue-eating louse do?

rq.p: How does it get into the fish?

cards.why: It's the only known parasite to functionally replace a host's organ.

cards.b: The mimic octopus of Southeast Asia can contort its body and arms to look like other animals, including venomous lionfish, sea snakes and flatfish. It seems to choose the disguise to suit the predator nearby.

q.p: Which animal can impersonate lionfish and sea snakes?

rq.p: Why does it mimic venomous animals?

cards.why: Predators avoid animals that look dangerous.

cards.b: In a 2006 study, an Asian elephant named Happy repeatedly touched a mark on her head that she could only see in a mirror. Passing this mirror test is rare: great apes, dolphins and some birds are among the few others.

q.p: What did Happy the elephant do in the mirror test?
o: Touched a mark only visible in the mirror

rq.p: What does passing the mirror test suggest?

cards.why: Few animals recognise their own reflection.

cards.t: Pigeons can tell Monet from Picasso
cards.b: In a 1995 study, Japanese researchers trained pigeons to peck when shown paintings by Monet or by Picasso. The birds then correctly told apart paintings by the two artists they had never seen before.

q.p: What could pigeons tell apart in a 1995 study?

rq.p: Could they sort paintings they'd never seen?

cards.why: Pigeons have excellent visual pattern recognition.

cards.b: Hippos secrete a reddish fluid from their skin, once mistaken for 'blood sweat'. It's neither blood nor sweat: it contains pigments that absorb ultraviolet light and seem to help fight bacteria.

q.p: What is a hippo's red 'blood sweat'?

rq.p: What else might the fluid do?

cards.why: Hippos spend hours in strong African sun.

cards.t: Flying fish glide hundreds of metres
cards.b: Flying fish build speed underwater, burst out and spread large wing-like fins to glide. By flicking their tail on the surface they can stretch flights to hundreds of metres, escaping predators below.

q.p: How do flying fish stay in the air?

rq.p: Why do flying fish leave the water?

cards.why: Tail flicks on the surface relaunch the glide.
